highlights.title: Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts
highlights.summary: ‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts. You’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.
body: “They don’t need your password, they don’t trigger a login alert, and they can often bypass your multifactor authentication (MFA).”
It looks like a regular session on the web. At some point you will have logged in and given your password, and maybe used MFA to prove it’s you.

If it’s a social media or email account you may discover it’s been used by scammers to trick other people. If it’s your bank they could access your account, or they could use details they find to perpetrate an impersonation scam.
And if you were shopping online, the fraudsters could change and redirect your order and charge it to your saved payment details.

highlights.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
highlights.summary: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by…
body: Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.

The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.
The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

highlights.title: 23 Years Later, Spike's Best 'Buffy' Quote Is Still One of the Best Lines in TV History
highlights.summary: Buffy ’s writers gave Spike some of the show’s sharpest one-liners — who could forget “Out. For. A. Walk. Bitch.”? But his best line comes in the series finale, “Chosen.” It’s the natural culmination of a character pulled between heroism and selfishness for most of his life, and it captures the…
body: Buffy the Vampire Slayer has no shortage of great characters. Buffy, Willow, Anya, and the rest of the Scoobies offer something for every kind of viewer, whether you’re here for the jokes, the crushes, or a character arc that unfolds over several seasons. But Spike (James Marsters) is in a league of his own. He’s beloved as both a villain and a love interest, and over the course of the series, he becomes one of its most complicated characters.

As Buffy and her allies battle the demons pouring out of the Hellmouth, the cavern starts to collapse. The others flee, trying to escape Sunnydale before the town is swallowed by the earth. Spike stays behind, using a magical amulet to keep the demons from getting out. Buffy asks him to leave with her, but he’s already made his choice. She reaches for his hand and tells him, “I love you.”

It’s a moment Spike has been hoping for over the past two seasons, perhaps longer. But he understands what Buffy means — and what she doesn’t. “No, you don’t. But thanks for saying it,” he replies. His sacrifice closes the Hellmouth and saves the world, making it the finale’s most emotional and consequential moment.

highlights.summary: In the third article in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the Ettinger factory in Walsall. ‘Our town is making jeans again’: reviving jobs and skills in Wales. From feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze.
body: “It is all down to attention to detail and everything we do is based around that.”

Gary Billingham is demonstrating how the 28 pieces which make up an Ettinger wallet are cut from leather using a hydraulic press by the small team at one of Walsall’s last remaining leather goods factories. The edges of the pieces are thinned down so they are ready to be turned, glued and stitched together by hand.

Billingham has been at the factory near Birmingham since the 1980s, when “there were three pages in the Yellow Pages” business directory listing leather factories in the West Midlands town. “They were everywhere. It has gone from that to about five factories. It is more like a cottage industry.”
About 20 people, mostly women, work carefully and precisely in Ettinger’s factory – a site of leather goods production since the 1890s – with a handful more doing work from home.

It is a cautionary tale about unchecked power, nestled within a vast setting with several dense subplots. David Lynch tried to make sense of Herbert’s saga in his flawed 1984 adaptation, while Alejandro Jodorowsky was unsuccessful in bringing his eccentric vision for Dune to life.
“There is no escape — we pay for the violence of our ancestors.”

Dune is many things: an allegory for ecological devastation and an epic space opera about the rise and fall of dynasties. Most importantly, it is about the dangers posed by charismatic leaders. highlights.title: The hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic - it needs to go. No regards, Tom | Tom Gill
highlights.summary: The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end. Enough! If email were a person, it would be an adult dressed in a teenager’s clothes, desperately trying to stay relevant.
body: Whereas other forms of communication have long since dispensed with unnecessary textual tassels, email communication styles still lean closer to telegram than a text. Since I last checked, almost no one relishes receiving a new email – unless it’s informing you of a significant cash windfall that means you can, in fact, now quit your job and stop using it altogether. Yet, for some reason, many people start their responses with “Thank you for your email!” I would put this forward as one of the least convincing sentences in the English language.

At the other end of the page is one of the most common yet totally unnecessary habits of the digital age: the email signoff. For those who haven’t yet realised, I’m here to tell you that you don’t need to sign your name at the end of an email – I can already see it’s from you. I know your name. Outlook has gone to extraordinary lengths to tell me your name. It’s in my inbox, the “from” field and the thread, and I probably begrudgingly addressed my last email directly to you.

highlights.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
highlights.summary: Security researchers used AI tools to help uncover years-old vulnerabilities in the PHP web scripting language. Then the AI-assisted attacks began.
body: As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.
So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

body: A specially commissioned china plate was also handed over by the town’s mayor before the 41-year-old Matthews, who was famously teetotal, gave a short speech. “He might have had a double carrot juice that day,” says his son, Stanley Matthews Jr, who will attend this year’s awards with his sister, Jean, and her two daughters. “There was no ceremony. ‘Here’s your Ballon d’Or, well done’, sort of thing. The switch of venue to England from its usual home in Paris is a mark of respect to the man who became the first active player to receive a knighthood in 1965, a few months before retiring at the age of 50. highlights.title: Carving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head on
highlights.summary: Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future. It’s the worst ski resort nightmare: hillsides of shaggy yellow grass streaked with slush under a leaden sky that’s coughing up sleet.
body: Not everywhere, of course. Only lower altitudes are seeing such disasters. Higher up, normal service continues. I’m in the Swiss resort of Laax, where most of the slopes are at about 2,000 metres, lofty enough to be snow-secure, for now. The halfpipe is busy with dudes in baggy trousers and headphones nonchalantly practising their double corks. On the traditional pistes there are four-year-olds who could probably ski before they could walk. And then – Switzerland has its wacky side – three young men in first-world-war greatcoats on antique wooden skis propel themselves with rough-hewn quarter-staves.

Is all this destined to disappear, perhaps in our children’s lifetimes? To put it in stark, white and black terms: are ski resorts in the same predicament as oil-dependent desert states, watching their one key source of wealth dwindle and disappear?

highlights.title: Blue Planet III is keeping the rough edges in the age of AI
highlights.summary: BBC's Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real.
body: BBC’s Blue Planet III is keeping in shots that would normally end up on the cutting room floor to prove it’s real.

Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans.

The series features incredible displays of dolphins trapping fish by plugging holes with sea sponges, inter-species fish communication, and 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”

highlights.title: Greg Wise on how he and Emma Thompson coped with failed IVF: ‘We hit an existential crisis – she was not a proper woman and I was not a proper man’
highlights.summary: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time. “I’m afraid this cycle has not been successful.” Emma and I cannot catch each other’s eye. We sit mute in our grief in the silence of the IVF doctor’s office.
body: Each cycle, each time we sat in that office, we had to ignore our grief and concentrate wholeheartedly and positively on our next attempt. We didn’t access any help over this time. We didn’t seek out counselling as a couple. I had no knowledge of how to process my grief – compounded month on month. Further cycles, more drugs, more fertility hormones, more ovarian hyperstimulation, injections, scans, blood tests came and went, all proving unsuccessful. I supported all wholeheartedly, but Emma was devastated by her inability to conceive again. In her mind, she had failed and could not forgive herself for that failure. And nothing I could say would change her point of view.
Her deep grief took her away. I had to deny mine. Try to comfort her rather than myself. Such is the lot of the self-appointed saviour.

body: Kim Kardashian and Kris Jenner have a shared affinity for archival fashion and high-octane glamour, with an increasing penchant for mother-daughter twinning. But their latest red carpet outing came with a particularly storied piece of Hollywood history, involving Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and a certain astrological sign of the moment.

At the Rome Film Festival last night, where Kardashian was celebrating the season two premiere of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama All’s Fair, Jenner arrived in a sweeping black velvet hooded cape, its ivory silk lining framing her face and glittering scorpions embroidered across the chest. She wore it with long white gloves and a floor-length white gown underneath.
The striking design was a homage to a Tiziani Roma creation worn by Elizabeth Taylor in 1969, when the actor attended Princess Grace of Monaco’s 40th birthday celebrations.

highlights.title: Supercell hit by cyberattack, but says no player data was affected
highlights.summary: The Clash of Clans developer says it was the target of multiple attacks last week and has notified police and regulators.
body: Supercell has confirmed that an unauthorised party has accessed a platform Supercell used to host company meetings and presentations.

In an announcement on October 21, the Clash of Clans developer said it was targeted by multiple cyberattacks last week, one of which caused the incident. Based on its investigations so far, Supercell believes no player data was affected.

It says it blocked further access, took the service offline and began investigating the platform and its security experts. It has since filed a police report, submitted a notification under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, and notified the Data Protection Ombudsman, but said that because the investigation is ongoing, it cannot share further details at this time.

The videos include current and former employees, as well as some guests and partners who took part in internal events. They may contain people’s names, images and voices, and the names and email addresses of the platform’s users were also accessed.

body: Anthropic has been sued by the owners of Elvis Presley ‘s music for allegedly utilizing his songs to train AI models without permission.
Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Presley, filed the lawsuit alongside other entities that also own rights to the “Jailhouse Rock” singer, according to Billboard.

In August, Round Hill sued Suno and Anthropic, claiming mass copyright infringement. They alleged the AI companies used hundreds of the publisher’s songs to train their AI models without permission. Anthropic was also previously sued by Universal Music Publishing, Abcko, Concord and BMG for similar claims of lyrics being utilized to train Claude, an AI agent.
Rolling Stone reports that the suit is seeking $150,000 per infringed song.
